subject: Chi-square tests and the independence of data points

messages.author: 3edc58ee737edd94
messages.subject: Chi-square tests and the independence of data points
parts:
Hi all

I would like your opinion on when (not) to use chi-square tests and
what to use instead (if possible in R, which is why I post this here).
The issue is this: it is well-known that the chi-square test for
independence in two-dimensional tables requires that the expected cell
frequencies are not too small (the exact limits proposed differ across
publications) and that the data points are independent of each other.
With regard to the latter point, I am a little curious (and I
apologize in advance if this is a dumb question). In a study that is
currently written up, a co-author and I look at the correlation
between the choice of one of several adverbs (the dep. variable) and
two categorical independent variables. The occurrences of the adverbs
coded for the two ind. vars. are from two corpora.

Now, on the one hand, one could say these data points are not
independent because one author may have contributed more than one data
point by using one or more adverbs more than once, and this seems to
be the line of reasoning of Woods, Fletcher, and Hughes (1986) or
Davis (2002).

On the other hand, I am thinking, well sure, there may be a dependency
relation / influence between successive uses of the adverbs (e.g.,
some kind of persistence effect similar to syntactic priming or what
not), but that is certainly not the null hypothesis. The null
hypothesis says "there is no effect, there is no relation, ..." so the
assumption of the data points not being independent is an alternative
hypothesis, and whoever posits that alternative hypothesis would have
to show that it is most likely correct. Thus, the burden of proof
would lie with the person who says "You can't use chi-square here" and
he would have to basically show that there is a significant relation
between adverbs that may be dozens or even hundreds of sentences apart
(in our data set or one similar enough).

Again, sry if this is a dumb question, but I am curious to hear what
you think about this. Thx,
STG
--
Stefan Th. Gries

messages.author: f6f55bd5390777ad
messages.subject: Re: [CorpLing with R] Chi-square tests and the independence of data points
parts:
Hi Stefan,

Great dumb question, I've broken my head over it more than once. Here's my dumb answer: as far as I can see the requirement of independence has nothing to do with the null-hypothesis that you formulate (here: absence of priming effects, right?) but with the fact that there is no equiprobability of occurrence if observations are not independent. Put differently: the priming issue seems secondary to me. If there is equiprobability, there should not be priming effects as all authors are equally represented. If there is no equiprobability, there might be priming effects and your analysis needs to take that into account. Unless you prefer to be sorry over being safe.

I think that you can avoid the complication (well, to some extent) by not allowing more than one example per author in your sample or you can deal with the complication by fitting more "advanced" models than "simple" chi-square. Actually, here's an issue I've been wondering about for quite some time: given the nature of corpus data that always includes multiple items produced by multiple subjects, should we ever fit plain easy basic regression models or is it always better to fit mixed effect models to capture the variance that is no doubt escaping our (also without doubt) cunningly selected predictor variables if we prefer being safe over being sorry? Thoughts welcome ....

Different from Stefan, I sure hope there is someone on this list for whom this question is dumb ;-)
Dagmar

messages.author: 3edc58ee737edd94
messages.subject: Re: [CorpLing with R] Re: Chi-square tests and the independence of data points
parts:
Hi

Thx for these comments, which will give me something to think about.
There is one thing I need to clarify though. You said:

> as far as I can see the requirement of independence has nothing to do with the null-hypothesis that you formulate (here: absence of priming effects, right?) but with the fact that there is no equiprobability of occurrence if observations are not independent.

Yes, with "null hypothesis" I meant the absence of priming effects. I
was also thinking, however, that if that null hypothesis is correct,
then priming is absent and that in turn means that the chi-square test
would test the following hypotheses (with the computation of the
expected frequencies untainted by priming effects):

H0: The independent variable X does not correlate with the choice of an adverb.
H1: The independent variable X correlates with the choice of an adverb.

Also, however, if you are correct,

- how do we define the level at which the data points are independent?
do two data points have to be from different corpus files to be
independent? or is it enough when they are from different parts of the
same corpus file (like when a BNC files contains text from different
newspaper files)? but what if text B is a response to text A and takes
up (even if only in paraphrase) linguistic material from A - is that
then dependent? Or, for spoken data: are two data points already
independent when they are from different speakers? or can they be
dependent even if they are from different speakers (for example
because they are from two adjacent conversational turns of two
speakers? how can this be operationalized properly?
- does that mean that the zillion of chi-square tests in corpus
linguistics where anyone speaker contributes more than one instance
are (at least conceptually) flawed because we always categorically
assume any (often unspecifiable) kind of priming influence between the
any two data points of one speaker?

I'd be interested in any further thoughts anyone might be willing to
share ... any ideas?

Thx,
STG

messages.author: 2ad9b08fa36a7ebd
messages.subject: Statistics is not an exact sciene
parts: My provocative 5c ;-)

Dagmar Divjak wrote:
>
> I think that you can avoid the complication (well, to some extent) by
> not allowing more than one example per author in your sample

but why draw the line here? Following this logic (and given what we
think we know about 'community grammars' etc), should we really allow,
then, more than one response per 'idiolect type' / 'dialect' / 'accent',
or even 'language'? What about the species -- one might even take the
stance (which is admittedly somewhat ridiculous ...) that there is an
innate language organ, which would have (wouldn't it?) grave
implications for the assumption of independence and equiprobability ...

And let's have a look at some other disciplines that rely on 'plain
regression' all the time -- quantitative sociology, public opinion
research, economics. These draw, more often than not, on surveys that
never have more than one response per subject/informant, all right, but
still they sample multiple responses from subjects of the same ethnicity
/ age bracket / SES / etc. So strictly speaking, such responses are not
independent, and plain regression is inappropriate -- is it not?

-Ben

messages.author: f6f55bd5390777ad
messages.subject: Re: [CorpLing with R] Re: Chi-square tests and the independence of data points
parts:
hi ben and stefan,

i totally agree, that 's why i wrote "(to some extent)" :-( the problem really is "where do we draw the line"?

i do think it would be great to come to an intial consensus about this. i guess, easiest would be to take "other" disciplines as an example, so shall we start there? we can then go on to discussing issues of independence and breaking our heads about operationalization ...

basically: i don't see how we can justify applying weaker selection procedures than other disciplines while fitting simpler models.
to me it *seems* that allowing only one example per author resembles the procedures followed in other sciences best, i.e. one answer per subject but multiple subjects from the same age group etc. if we don't do *at least* that, we definitely shouldn't use the basic models. it is "not done" in "other" discplines either: as soon as they have multiple people doing multiple things, corrections are in order. this *doesn't* mean we can't use multiple examples from one subject, it "just" means we should take the multiple measurements per subject into account when analyzing the data. you might still find that there is no subject-effect, in which case you can run the simpler model, i guess. but i think, to be safe, you should first check. this also *doesn't* mean that taking one example per subject guarantees independence ... i think many of the things stefan list *might* be issues, eg A taking up material from B, or A replying to B ...

anyone any more cents to spare?
dagmar

Yes, that is a very good point. This issue of where to draw the line
*on a principled basis* is just terrible ... I have no idea of how far
one would have to go with making such distinctions or how far-reaching
the implications would be (although I am currently working on this).

Dagmar Divjak wrote:
> basically: i don't see how we can justify applying weaker selection procedures than other disciplines while fitting simpler models.

Yes, in a way that does seem like the obvious approach but does hardly
anybody do that?
(i) Because people (and obviously I include myself here - after all, I
posted this question) aren't familiar enough with all this? (Part of
the reason for this may be that even some refs don't discuss that
issue in detail: Woods, Fletcher, and Hughes (1986) caution the reader
but don't say what to do instead of chi-square tests, Davis (2002)
says that with regard to his example, stats are not needed anyway so
provides no real alternative ...);
(ii) because it is too hard to come up with a principled answer to the
question when something is independent and when it is not?
(iii) ...?

messages.author: 2ad9b08fa36a7ebd
messages.subject: Re: [CorpLing with R] Re: Chi-square tests and the independence of data points
parts:
Dagmar Divjak wrote:
> basically: i don't see how we can justify applying weaker selection
> procedures than other disciplines while fitting simpler models.

Well I guess it really all depends on your specific research interest
and, crucially, on your assumptions.

If I want to generalize about _one speaker_ (not about a speech
community, the universe, etc.), it is IMHO legit to fit a plain
regression model based on multiple responses from that speaker.

If you additionally assume a 'community grammar' or something like that
(while not seeking to make claims about the universe, of course), it
seems to me that it's also legit to regress multiple responses from more
than one speaker. This sort of stuff is what's underlying much of the
(Labovian) variationist sociolinguistic literature, and while I sure
think their specific method (i.e. VARBRUL) is flawed, I'd hesitate to
damn the whole methodology.

-Ben
